name: Public Blockchain
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Public Blockchains: When Anyone Can Read the Ledger Too
lesson.summary: A public blockchain is one whose full transaction history is visible to anyone, a separate design choice from permissionless participation that most well known networks happen to combine.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter drew a line between permissioned and permissionless blockchains based on who is allowed to participate and validate. Public blockchain answers a related but distinct question: who is allowed to read the ledger's contents. A network is public when anyone, whether or not they hold any funds on it or run a node, can inspect the full history of transactions and current state without asking anyone's permission.

In practice, Bitcoin and Ethereum are both permissionless and public, which is why the two labels get used almost interchangeably in casual conversation, even though they describe different things. Anyone can open a block explorer, a website that reads directly from the blockchain, and look up any address's balance, every transaction it has ever sent or received, and the exact block each one was confirmed in, all without creating an account or requesting access from anyone. This transparency is a direct consequence of how these networks achieve consensus: every validating node needs to see the same transaction data to agree on the same ledger state, and since anyone can run a node on a permissionless network, that same data ends up visible to the public as a side effect.

This transparency serves a real purpose beyond curiosity. It enables independent verification, sometimes called auditability, where any outside party can check that the rules of the system were actually followed rather than trusting a company's internal books or a bank's word that a transaction cleared. That is a meaningful shift from traditional finance, where verifying a claim about your own balance usually means trusting the institution that holds the record. The trade off is privacy: public visibility means every transaction flow is exposed to anyone who looks, and while addresses are pseudonymous rather than directly tied to a name, patterns of activity linked to a single address can often be traced and, in some cases, connected back to a real identity through exchanges or other services that do require identification.

It is useful to keep public and permissionless conceptually separate, even though real world networks usually pair them the same way. A network could, in principle, be permissionless to validate while keeping transaction contents encrypted or otherwise hidden from casual observers, or permissioned to validate while still publishing enough information, sometimes cryptographic proofs rather than raw data, for outsiders to check that something happened without seeing the details. These combinations are uncommon, but recognizing them as separate axes clarifies what is actually being promised when a network calls itself public, private, permissioned, or permissionless, rather than treating those words as a single package deal.

With that distinction in hand, the next chapter turns to private blockchains, which typically pair permissioned participation with restricted read access as well, controlled by a single organization rather than the open public.
